# Web3 Does Not Have One Customer. That Is Why Most Launch Plans Break.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/web3-multi-audience-launch-plan/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-25 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A Web3 product can attract thousands of people to a launch announcement and still have almost nobody using it a month later, because it reached an audience but not the people needed to make it work. A protocol may need users, developers, capital providers, distribution partners, institutions and governance participants, each waiting for evidence from someone else. Map those groups, launch in the order the dependencies require, keep one product truth explained differently for each, and measure participation rather than attention.

## Key points

- A protocol is a market with several sides; a single announcement to "the community" answers none of their questions.
- Write down each group's role and what it needs before it can take part.
- Sequence by dependency: readiness, then proof, then distribution.
- One product truth, explained four ways; MiCA requires marketing to be consistent with the white paper.
- A launch is coordinated when one group's participation makes the next group's more likely.

Unlike a simple consumer app, a protocol may need several groups to participate before it works as intended. Users, developers, liquidity providers, ecosystem partners and institutions may each be waiting for evidence from someone else. A launch plan should solve those dependencies, not simply announce to everyone at once.

The evidence that announcements alone do not create usage is now well documented. Academic analysis of nine major airdrops found activity rose temporarily but lasting engagement did not follow, and after Arbitrum's airdrop, transactions per address fell even as total fees rose. Attention arrived. Most of the participants the network needed did not stay.

## Start with the people who make the product work

Six groups recur across Web3 launches. Not every project needs all six. A wallet app and a regulated asset platform have very different needs.

| Group | Role in the system | What it needs before it acts | Typical first measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Users | Use the product | A clear reason to try it, what it costs, how to exit | First meaningful action; return within 30 days |
| Developers and integrators | Build on or connect to it | Current documentation, a reliable integration path, support | Successful integrations in production |
| Capital and liquidity providers | Make it usable at size | Risk disclosure, audits, economic terms | Committed against actively used capital, and how long it stays |
| Distribution partners | Bring their customers | What they gain, support obligations, demand evidence | Qualified introductions and downstream use |
| Institutions | Allocate, custody or list | Operating, compliance and accountability information | Diligence completed; first allocation |
| Community and governance | Sustain and steer it | A reason to take part, real decisions to make | Contributors and proposals with participation |

Write down the role each group plays. That is more useful than treating everyone as a single group called "the community". The same announcement is unlikely to answer all of those questions. The same logic applies in B2B selling, where the several members of a [buying committee](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/) each need different evidence before a deal moves.

## Launch in the order your product actually needs

Consider a hypothetical tokenised asset platform. A broad marketing campaign might create awareness, but it would not replace custody arrangements, onboarding requirements or a way for investors to access the product.

A sensible sequence might be: confirm the legal and custody model; secure an anchor distribution or liquidity partner; test onboarding with a limited group; document the issues; and only then expand public promotion. The exact order depends on the business. The principle is to identify what must be true before the next audience can act.

- **First, readiness:** what needs to work for the first users or partners to take part.
- **Next, proof:** which successful integration, product action or operating result would make another group comfortable.
- **Then, distribution:** who can bring more of the right participants once that proof exists.

Regulation has made the readiness step more concrete in 2026. In the EU, MiCA's transitional period ended on 1 July 2026, and ESMA told unauthorised service providers to stop onboarding EU clients and stop marketing to them immediately. For a platform that depends on an exchange, custodian or broker to reach EU users, the partner's authorisation status is now a launch dependency, not a detail. In the US, the SEC's March 2026 interpretation clarified which tokens fall outside securities law, while its proposed Regulation Crypto Assets, published in August 2026, is still a proposal. Institutions will ask where a product sits under both. Get counsel; this is not legal advice.

> A launch is not coordinated because every account posted on the same day. It is coordinated when one group's participation makes the next group's more likely.

## Keep one product truth, but change the explanation

Suppose the product makes it easier to access a particular financial instrument. A user wants to know what they can do and what it costs. A wallet integration team wants implementation details. A partner wants to understand demand and support obligations. An institution wants documentation, risk controls and accountability.

The product should not tell four contradictory stories. It should explain one real capability in four useful ways. For each audience, write down the claim, the evidence, the next action and the main reason they might hesitate. If the evidence does not exist yet, say that internally rather than filling the gap with marketing language. Our piece [one truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) sets out the method, and [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) covers how to choose the truth in the first place.

Consistency is also a legal expectation. MiCA Article 7 requires crypto-asset marketing communications to be fair, clear and not misleading and consistent with the white paper, and bars marketing before a required white paper is published. The SEC's 2026 interpretation turns on what an issuer promised, when and through which medium, and Chairman Atkins said promises that create reliance "must be explicit and unambiguous". A deck that tells investors one thing and a community post that implies another is a positioning problem and a disclosure problem at once.

## Use a 90-day plan as a sequence, not a countdown

| Phase | Work | Exit test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Days 1 to 30 | Interview the participants who matter most; identify blockers; test approved claims; make the first integration or onboarding reliable; define success | Named first users and partners; one working path end to end |
| Days 31 to 60 | Work with a small group of real users and partners; run developer sessions or walkthroughs; turn objections into documentation and product fixes | Repeat use from the first group; recurring objections answered in docs |
| Days 61 to 90 | Expand the channels and groups showing genuine activity; announce partnerships that create access or utility; use creators and community programming to explain what people already need help with | Activity growing in groups the next one depends on |

This is an illustrative sequence, not a promise that any Web3 project can reach launch readiness in exactly 90 days. Our [build order for crypto and digital assets](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-crypto-and-digital-assets/) covers the commercial record the team should keep through it.

## Measure useful participation, not just attention

Different participants need different measures: for users, a first meaningful action and whether they return; for developers, successful integrations; for capital providers, committed against actively used capital and its persistence; for partners, qualified introductions and downstream product use. Link those outcomes to the cost of acquiring them where possible.

Capital providers will also judge risk, and the record gives them reason to. Chainalysis estimated over $3.4 billion was stolen in crypto hacks in 2025. A launch plan that reaches liquidity providers before audits are named and dated asks them to take a risk the team has not yet reduced. Our piece on [the user story before the token story](https://lowob.com/research/the-user-story-before-the-token-story/) covers what each audience needs to see.

## lowob takeaways

- **Map the actual participants.** Do not treat users, builders, capital and partners as one audience.
- **Find the dependency chain.** Make the thing the next group needs to trust or use before inviting them.
- **Tailor the proof, not the truth.** Each group needs different evidence for the same consistent claim.
- **Measure continuing use.** A successful announcement is not the same as a working market.

## Common questions

### How do you plan a Web3 product launch?

List the groups the product needs, such as users, developers, liquidity providers, partners and institutions, and what each needs before acting. Sequence the launch by dependency: readiness first, then proof, then wider distribution.

### Who are the audiences for a crypto protocol launch?

Usually some of six groups: users, developers and integrators, capital and liquidity providers, distribution partners, institutional stakeholders, and community or governance participants. Not every project needs all six.

### Can a crypto project tell investors and users different stories?

It should explain one product truth differently for each, but never contradict itself. MiCA requires marketing to be consistent with the white paper, and US analysis of tokens turns on what issuers promised in public.

### How do you measure a Web3 launch?

By participation for each group: first meaningful actions and returns for users, live integrations for developers, actively used capital for liquidity providers, and qualified introductions for partners, linked to acquisition cost where possible.
